name: WSJ0-2mix
ability_definition: The ability to focus on a single source of sound in the presence of other distracting sounds.

task_realism.reasoning: Recovering speakers from overlapping speech is the core 'cocktail party' problem that auditory attention addresses. But the mixtures are synthetic sums of read Wall Street Journal sentences, not conversational speech. Real workplace listening (a call-center agent with background chatter, a dispatcher, someone on a factory floor, a meeting participant) involves spontaneous speech, varied distractors and a need to follow one person over time.

evaluation_conditions.reasoning: Conditions are highly idealized. The audio is clean, anechoic, single-channel and 8 kHz. There are exactly two speakers mixed at controlled 0-5 dB relative levels, with no reverberation, ambient noise, microphone variation, overlapping non-speech events or real-time/streaming constraints. The input distribution is far narrower and easier than the acoustic environments where workers must focus on one sound source.

construct_coverage.reasoning: The benchmark covers only a narrow slice of the ability: speech-on-speech separation with two talkers. It omits cue-driven selection of a target, because it separates all sources rather than attending to one. It also omits non-speech distractors (machinery, alarms, music), larger numbers of competing sources, sustained attention over long interactions, and any downstream comprehension of the attended source.

format_match.reasoning: The input is a real audio waveform, which resembles a real artifact. The output, however, is a set of reconstructed waveforms scored by SI-SDRi, a signal-fidelity metric. Real work requires understanding or acting on the attended source, such as transcribing, responding or detecting a cue. Signal reconstruction quality correlates only loosely with that kind of functional attention.

transferability_reasoning: WSJ0-2mix directly targets the canonical overlapping-speech form of auditory attention, but it does so under clean, anechoic, two-speaker, read-speech conditions with a signal-fidelity metric. It also asks for separation of all sources rather than focus on a cued target. Strong scores therefore say little about focusing on one sound source amid the noisy, reverberant, multi-source distractions of real workplaces, so transfer is limited.

2020.metric: SI-SNRi (scale-invariant signal-to-noise ratio improvement), dB; higher is better
2020.human_reference: General working adults with normal hearing who must follow one talker among competing talkers (e.g., open offices, meetings, customer-facing roles).

2022.human_reference: General adult population with normal hearing, the people who use auditory attention at work to follow one talker among others (meetings, call centers, noisy workplaces).

2023.metric: SI-SDRi (dB, scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio improvement; higher is better)
2023.human_reference: General adult working population with normal hearing (people who routinely must follow one talker among competing voices, e.g., in offices, meetings, customer-facing and control-room settings)
